messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes 
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)
- Forbidden causal connections that must never appear

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT include inactive components — these are clinically irrelevant for this patient and must not be mentioned.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- For forbidden pairs, never use explicit causal language between them in a single sentence:
  "led to", "caused", "as a result of", "because of", "driven by", "resulting in".
  Both components may appear in the same paragraph — just not causally linked in one sentence.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Children Present: Being around children, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam Weber was 26 when a flash flood tore through the campground where he, his wife, and her young niece had gone for a weekend trip. The rain had been hard all afternoon, but he had told himself they would be fine. By nightfall the water came fast, carrying mud, branches, and pieces of shattered gear through the cabins. What stayed with him were not clean, orderly memories but broken flashes: the sour smell of soaked clothes and sweat in the crush of bodies trying to move uphill, a child screaming for her mother, his wife slipping from his grasp in the dark water. When he tries to describe that night now, he stops and stares at the floor. He knows what happened, but the words will not come in sequence. Instead, the scene returns like a film clip that starts before he is ready and repeats without finishing.

In the months after the flood, those fragments began attaching themselves to ordinary moments. At work as a salesperson in a busy home improvement store, the smell of a customer’s body odour after a long day in the heat can pull him straight back into the panic of the evacuation. If children come through his aisle, especially if one calls out loudly or starts to cry, the memory jumps forward in disconnected pieces—the small hand he could not keep hold of, the noise, the water. Even talking about the flood in the break room is enough to set the replay going. Each time this happens, Liam’s mind lands on the same conclusion: he was inadequate when it mattered most. He had come to believe that if he had been stronger, faster, more capable, his wife might still be alive.

That belief has hardened rather than softened. The more the memories replay in fragments, the more certain he becomes that something in him failed catastrophically. He also cannot stop circling around the fact that no one, in his view, has really been held accountable: the campground reopened, the warnings had been poor, and life seemed to continue for everyone else. The event feels unfinished, senseless. From there it does not take much for him to think, with bitter conviction, that he cannot deal with even minor upset now. A delayed text, a late delivery, a coworker not showing up on time—small disruptions feel like proof that he is already near the edge.

That sense of fragility has shaped how he lives. Liam tries hard to control his emotions, especially around other people. If he feels himself getting tight in the chest or watery-eyed, he clamps down, changes the subject, or leaves the room. He avoids grief reminders with a carefulness that has grown over time: he keeps his wife’s photo turned face down on a shelf, takes a longer route through town to avoid the park where they used to walk, and will not look at camping displays in the store unless he has to. At home he sometimes drifts off into elaborate fantasy, losing himself in imagined versions of life where the trip was canceled or the water never rose. Those habits give him brief distance, but they also leave the loss and the flood strangely unprocessed, so that the memory returns in the same jagged, wordless form. Afterward he feels even more defective for not being able to face what happened directly.

The replaying memories have also changed his sense of safety. Because they arrive so suddenly and vividly, he stays on guard even inside his apartment, checking the windows during storms and listening for changes in the weather app notification tone on his phone. He is quick to anger in ways that embarrass him: snapping at a neighbor over hallway noise, slamming a cabinet when an online order runs late, barking at a customer who asked for help while a child tugged at the cart nearby. Delays are especially hard. If his manager is late back from lunch or a friend does not answer right away, Liam is certain something bad is happening. In that keyed-up state, he scans more intensely for signs of danger, and the very things he is watching for—children’s voices, sweat, any conversation about the flood—stand out immediately and hit harder.

Over time, this constant readiness has fed his view of himself. His irritability and vigilance seem to him like more evidence that he is no longer someone who can cope, just someone damaged and unpredictable. He has started turning down shifts on family-shopping weekends to avoid being around children, and his sales numbers have slipped because he leaves the floor when a smell or conversation catches him off guard. Friends have stopped asking him to join gatherings because he goes silent or disappears. He finally came for help after a storm warning sent him pacing his apartment all night, unable to settle even after the rain passed, and he nearly shouted at a customer’s son the next morning when the boy started crying in his aisle. What frightens Liam most is the thought that this is permanent—that he failed once, broke in the flood, and will stay trapped in that night. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might find a way to remember his wife without being pulled under again.
